To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cries of hearing-impaired and normal hearing infants can be differentiated by means of signal analysis, and the results are consistent with the auditory findings.

the cry vocalizations of profoundly hearing-im- paired infants are different regarding the perceived sound, rhythm, and melody of the cries, and that these features may be used to automatically classify the cries.

(i) hearing-impaired infants cry differently from infants with normal hearing, (ii) this difference is due to the lack or reduced amount of auditory feedback, (iii) this difference can be observed and quantified using signal analysis techniques, (iv) it can be used to automatically detect hearing impairments in infants, (v) this detection is based on cry characteristics which are not related to the cause of the hearing impairment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the auditory and signal analysis of infant cries in order to detect hearing impairment at an early stage, and thus to improve the chances of successful hearing rehabilitation.
an auditory and signal analysis of infant cry vocalizations in the context of the early detection of congenital deafness.
the development of a diagnostic tool which can be used in addition to the standard diagnostic procedure for hearing impaired children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cries of hearing-impaired and normally hearing infants differ significantly.
hearing-impaired cries are not identical to those of infants with normal hearing abilities, and that the differences can be detected and classified by both auditory and automatic methods.
hearing-impaired infants produce cries with significantly different spectral, melodic and rhythmal characteristics, which can be detected by naive and expert listeners and by signal analysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cry vocalizations of profoundly hearing-im-paired infants differ significantly from the cries of infants with normal hearing.

cry vocalizations can be used as a diagnostic tool for the detection of hearing impairment in infants.

the cry production model, which is based on the assumption that the cry is produced as an auditory-motoric feedback loop, can be applied to explain the differences between the cries of infants with hearing impairment and normal hearing abilities.
